analytic.title: Optimizing the Deployment of Distributed Real-time Embedded Applications

div.p: The synthesis of a valid and optimized deployment model from functional and platform models is a crucial issue in the development of distributed real-time systems. The synthesis consists in the allocation of functions/signals to execution nodes/communication buses, the mapping of functions/signals into tasks/messages and the priority assignment to tasks/messages. Current approaches provide partial solutions for the synthesis of a deployment model on distributed platforms, as either the allocation or the mapping is fixed a-priori. In order to tackle this problem we propose an optimization technique, based on two different mathematical programming formulations, to handle optimization of both allocation and mapping. The optimization is multi-objective and considers extensibility maximization, latency minimization and minimization of the number of tasks. The obtained solutions satisfy timing and platform resources requirements. An automotive case study shows the effectiveness of our approach.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Today real-time applications are represented by a huge number of communicating software functions that must be running on distributed execution platforms. One important task of designers is to deploy functions and their interactions on the underlying execution platform while timing and platform requirements are respected.

Deployment consists in three phases: (i) allocating functions, resp. signals, on execution nodes, resp. communication buses, then (ii) mapping functions, resp. signals, to tasks, resp. messages (iii) and finally attributing priorities to tasks and messages.

The multiple deployment choices represent a strong motivation for providing guidance to designers during the deployment phase. Several approaches have been proposed to assist the designer in the synthesis of the deployment model, but none of them cover the entire problem. [1], [2] consider optimization techniques for only the allocation of tasks/messages to nodes/buses, without considering functional level. Authors in [3], [4], [5] focus on the mapping of This work has been partially supported by European Commission under the FP7 MAENAD project, grant agreement no. 260057. functions/signals into tasks/messages, with a priori-known allocation of functions on nodes.

In the present work, we propose an optimization technique to consider the whole deployment problem. The technique is based on two consecutive steps. In the first step, an allocation of functions/signals on execution nodes/communication buses is found. In the second step, the allocation found in the first step is taken as input, then priorities are assigned to functions/signals in order to group them in tasks/messages according to the assigned priorities.

As in [1], [2], the proposed technique is based on Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP). The proposal considers timing and platform resources constraints. As for metrics, we consider a multi-objective optimization which includes the minimization of latency and tasks number and the maximization of extensibility. For such technique, we introduce specific intermediate metrics for the first step.

The next section presents the different models involved in the deployment problem. Section III describes the twosteps deployment approach. Then, the section IV illustrates the approach on an automotive case study, evaluating its effectiveness. Last section concludes and gives a set of perspectives.

div.head: II. DEFINITION OF SYSTEM MODELS AND PROBLEM
FORMULATION
div.p: In this section the functional, the platform and the deployment models are formally defined along with the deployment problem.

div.head: A. Functional Model
div.p: The behavior of an embedded real-time application is represented by a directed acyclic graph based on the synchronous dataflow semantic [6]. This graph is composed of a set of concurrent linear transactions G={Γ 1 ,Γ 2 ,...,Γ p }. Each transaction is a tuple {F, Ω}, where F={f 1 ,f 2 ,...,f q } is the set of functions that represent the atomic operations of the application and Ω ={l 1 ,l 2 ,...,l l } is a set of links representing the interactions between functions. Functions exchange data signals through these links. Note Φ ={s 1 ,s 2 ,...,s s } the set of exchanged signals. A transaction Γ i is triggered by an external event e i that can be periodic or sporadic with, respectively, an activation period or a minimum inter-arrival time between activations, denoted P Γi . In addition, each transaction has a deadline D i that represents an application timing requirement. A function f i and a signal s i , have a time budget ω fi and ω si which determine respectively the upper bound on execution time and the transmission time. A function/signal has also a specific activation rate (P fi /P si ) which is the activation period of the transaction that possessed it. Activation model for functions/signals is the event-triggered model [7]. Figure 1 shows an example of a functional model.

div.head: B. Platform model
div.p: The platform model represents the hardware and software architecture of the system. Specifically, the hardware architecture is represented by a graph G including a set of execution nodes C={c 1 , c 2 , ..., c c } connected through communication buses β ={β 1 , β 2 ,..., β b }. Both the execution nodes and communication buses have a maximal utilization capacity, respectively μ c and μ β , that must not be exceeded. Execution nodes offer a maximal number of concurrent execution resources T={t c1 , t c2 , ..., t ct } called tasks. A task t i is used to execute a set of functions and it has some parameters which are (i) time budget denoted as ω ti , (ii) priority π ti and (iii) activation period P ti . In their turn, the communication buses propose a set of communication resources called communication tasks. A communication task is used to send a single message and each message may transfer signals or not, ψ ={m 1 , m 2 , ..., m m } represents the set of messages. Each message m i has some parameters as well, whic are: a priority π mi , a time budget ω mi and an activation period P ti . Each execution node runs a realtime operating system based on a preemptive fixed priority scheduling. Furthermore, a non-preemptive fixed priority scheduling is implemented on the communication buses, this corresponds to CAN buses1 . Figure 2 shows an example of a platform model.

div.head: C. Deployment model
div.p: The deployment model represents a particular configuration in which: each function/signal belonging to the functional model is assigned to a task/message offered

div.head: D. Problem statement: deployment model synthesis
div.p: Given a functional model provided with a set of optimization metrics ζ ={ς 1 ,ς 2 ,...,ς ς } ,chosen by the designer, and a platform model, we are interested in defining a deployment model such as it will respect platform utilization capacity and timing constraints. The deployment model should also be optimized with respect to (w.r.t.) the given set of metrics.
To define a deployment model, functions and exchanged signals should be mapped on the underlying platform resources then a configuration of platform resources should be given.

div.head: III. THE DESCRIPTION OF THE DEPLOYMENT APPROACH
div.p: To deal with the deployment problem, we propose an optimization technique based on two different MILP formulations. As shown in Figure 3, the first formulation tackles the first step, called the allocation step and the second one deals with the mapping and priority assignment step. In the following, constraints and optimization objectives are presented for the two steps. the maximum authorized load. During the allocation task, the load for each execution node and communication bus should be within the maximum authorised load. Allocation constraints. The allocation constraints are related to the application, it consists in the possibility of determining the allocation of a particular function. It also concerns signals, when there exist constraints such that the sender and receiver functions of the signal must be assigned to different execution nodes. The second step aims at grouping functions/signals into tasks/messages and at assigning priorities to the latter. For this step, we give another MILP formulation which aims at firstly assigning priorities to functions/signals and then, at grouping them on tasks/messages such that functions/signals with the same priority are assigned to the same task/message. In this formulation, we consider latency and harmonic periods constraints. Latency constraints. Latency represents the largest time required for the system to respond to an external stimulus. However, latency (timing) constraints consist in having latency for each transaction within its deadline. Harmonic rates constraints. These constraints express the fact that a task/message can contain only functions/signals with harmonic periods.

div.head: B. Optimization Objectives
div.p: In the present work, we consider a multi-objective optimization for the deployment problem. We choose task extensibility, tasks number and latency as target objectives. Task extensibility: the extensibility objective addresses the goal of accommodating, in the deployment model, possible future changes in tasks time budget without exceeding resource utilization constraints. Indeed, the increase of task time budget means the increase of time budgets of functions that are assigned to this task. Tasks number: this objective represents the number of tasks used to execute the application. It should be lower or equal to the maximum number offered by the execution platform. Latency: the optimization of this objective involves reducing the response time to an external stimulus, this makes the system faster.

Since some elements present in the second step are absent in the first step, like tasks and priorities, it is not possible to optimize all the cited objectives during the two steps. To address this problem, we need to define intermediate objectives for the allocation step while leading the final deployment towards an optimized one. These intermediate objectives are detailed below: Function extensibility: it represents the maximum possible increase in time budget of functions while utilization capacity of the execution nodes are not exceeded. The maximization of this objective guide the solution to a deployment optimized relative to task extensibility. Inter-nodes communication: it consists in minimizing communication over the buses. The minimization of this objective favours a deployment model optimized for latency as remote communication increases the latency. Interference: interference of a function represents the waiting time to access to the CPU of the execution node. This delay is caused by concurrent functions that belong to the same execution node. Two functions are concurrent if their execution are independent. The minimization of interference means increasing the parallelism, thus minimizing the latencies. Non-harmonic rates: this objective intends to minimize the case in which two functions with non-harmonic rates will be allocated on the same execution node in order to minimize the number of tasks in the final solution. This comes from the fact that two non-harmonic functions cannot be grouped together in the same task in the second step.

div.head: IV. DEPLOYMENT OF AN AUTOMOTIVE SYSTEM
div.p: The distributed real-time embedded system considered to illustrate our proposal is an automotive system which is the cruise control system (CCS). This system is presented in [9] for which response times for a given deployment model are shown. In this section, we show how the application of the optimization approach presented in section III to CCS finds other allocation/configurations for the deployment model that improve latency, extensibility and tasks number.

div.head: A. Presentation of cruise control system
div.p: The cruise control system (CCS) automatically stabilizes the vehicle speed according to the driver's desired set speed. Functional model of CCS is composed of two linear transactions, the first one contains six functions (Input acquisition, Input interpretation, Speed setpoint, Application condition, Basic function and Controller) and five signals, the second is formed by two functions (Diagnosis and Limp home) and one signal. The description of functions and system parameters are given in [10]. The hardware architecture of the platform model is composed of two Electronic control units (ECU), which represent execution nodes, (Body controller ECU and Engine management ECU) linked by one CAN bus.

div.head: B. Results and discussion
div.p: This paragraph presents the solution obtained when applying our approach to cruise control system and its comparison with the existing one. Note that we use GLPSOL [11] as MILP solver 2 . Figure 4 shows the existing solution presented in [9]. In this solution, the functions Input acquisition, Input interpretation and Diagnosis are allocated to Body controller ECU and the other functions (Speed setpoint, Application condition, Basic function, Controller and Limp home) are allocated to Engine management ECU. There are two tasks on each execution node and the tasks priorities are decreasing according to the following tasks ordering: Task2 with the highest priority, Task4, Task3, Task1. Table I shows the obtained results comparing to the existing solution. Our solution gives better extensibility and reduces tasks number and latency w.r.t. the original ones.

div.head: V. SUMMARY AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: We present in this paper an approach providing assistance to the real-time embedded applications designers during the 2 GLPSOL is a MILP solver included in GNU Linear Programming Kit (GLPK) and it is based on the branch-and-cut method.

synthesis of the deployment model. In this approach, we consider event-triggered activation model and we propose two MILP formulations for optimizing: the allocation of functions/signals to execution nodes, then the mapping of functions/signals on tasks/messages and tasks/messages priorities assignment. We take into account three optimization objectives which are extensibility maximization, latency and tasks number minimization. To evaluate the performance of our proposal, we test it on an automotive case study. To the best of our knowledge this is the first optimization technique which completely addresses the synthesis problem in this context. As for future work we are planning to experiment our approach on sized applications then extend it to more complex functional models. For instance, a functional model in which transactions are non-linear.
